- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤0.3), model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for volatility or panic-driven rebound.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days); apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 0.5–1.5% from forecast 2–3 days post-spike.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.67, 1.00, 0.33), model may misread momentum; apply mean reversion bias: forecast should align with 30-day moving average of history, not trend.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term mean reversion; if true outcome deviates >2% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast toward that average.
- When sentiment is high and price is rising, model tends to over-forecast; if sentiment >0.7 and price >75, cap forecast at +5% above current price.
- If sentiment is low and price is falling, model under-forecasts; if sentiment <0.3 and price <70, add 1–2% to forecast to account for “panic sell-off” or “recovery lag”.
